statewide.lead: In the news, the most widely reported reasons are poverty & child labour (24 of 30 districts) and child marriage & girls' exits (23). Child labour is named outright in 14 districts, though child marriage gets more headlines (35 against 12). In the UIDAI/NITI data, the district-level dominant factor for 32 of 35 Karnataka rows is the share of English-medium schools. They look like two answers to one question, but they are answers to two different questions.

methods.state: One factor is ranked highest for the whole state; each district's value is its own figure for that factor.
methods.district: A factor is selected for each district on its own; the value is that factor's fitted weight in the analysis, not a raw percentage.

generalClaims: Change in medium of instruction impacts student dropout
Students struggle to understand lessons in an unfamiliar language

differ.title: They answer different questions
differ.text: The data asks which measured school or household indicator best tracks the differences in dropout between districts. The news reports what pushes particular children out of school. A factor can track dropout across districts without being what families describe, and the other way round.

differ.title: The data cannot see child labour
differ.text: Across all 776 district rows in India, the workbooks name 23 different state-level and 39 district-level factors. Every one is a school-facility, teacher, inspection, household-amenity or women's-schooling indicator. None measures child labour, child marriage, migration or household income, so child labour could never come out as a data factor.

differ.title: News follows events
differ.text: Rescue raids, enforcement drives and NGO reports make stories, and each names a district. A school's language of instruction rarely does. Of the 17 child-labour reasons we found, 1 rests on strong evidence, 4 on moderate and 12 on thin. Child labour is widely mentioned, but the evidence behind each mention is usually thin.

differ.title: One indicator for almost every district
differ.text: English-medium share is the district-level factor for 32 of 35 Karnataka rows and for 263 of 776 districts nationally, the most common factor in India. When the same indicator is picked nearly everywhere, it behaves like a broad background marker rather than a local explanation. Its value is described as a fitted weight from the analysis, not a share of schools.

connect.text: Both can be true. The share of English-medium schools may track access to private and urban schooling and household means, which are the same conditions under which the news reports children working instead of studying. General research from elsewhere, found during our checks, also links a change in the medium of instruction, or lessons in an unfamiliar language, to students dropping out (2 page-verified claims, none about a Karnataka district).
connect.untested: We have not tested this. Our files hold neither each district's actual share of English-medium schools nor a district-level measure of child labour. Testing it would need both, analysed together against dropout.
